title: Lessons Learned from a Two-Round Delphi-based Scenario Study
author: Schmalz, Spinler, et al.

steps.title: Develop future projections
steps.instruction: Generate future projections by combining three qualitative methods—(1) a systematic literature review, (2) expert interviews, and (3) a single workshop—ensuring triangulation of sources and inclusion of industry representatives to capture practical perspectives.

steps.title: Define panelist criteria and identify candidates
steps.instruction: Establish pre‑selection criteria: diverse backgrounds, minimum two years’ work experience in the mobility industry, and a European working scope. Identify ten stakeholder groups covering all main travel segments. Locate potential panelists via personal networks, conference participant lists, and LinkedIn. Record each candidate’s name, country, position, contact details, response status, and comments in a table, assign a numeric ID starting at 1, and store the personal data securely (e.g., password‑protected files).

steps.title: Invite panelists and record responses
steps.instruction: Email 113 identified individuals with an invitation. Outcomes: 16 declined (time constraints, extended absence, or self‑assessed insufficient expertise), 8 agreed but either did not return questionnaires or submitted responses with many missing values, 41 gave no response, and 5 could not be contacted due to incorrect email addresses. Consequently, 43 panelists participated in round 1 (38 % response rate). Five dropped out before round 2, leaving 38 participants (overall response rate 34 %). Record expertise ratings (31 rated their expertise as “high” or “very high”) and gender distribution (39 % female).

steps.title: Conduct first Delphi round
steps.instruction: Send a short introductory email to each panelist with the questionnaire attached as a read‑only Word document. Allow a minimum of two weeks for return. Issue reminder emails and telephone calls as needed. After receipt, inspect raw data for missing values or duplicate answers; contact panelists to request corrected estimations. Collect 504 qualitative comments; split them into supporting and non‑supporting arguments using a simple Excel table. Perform descriptive statistics in R (calculate mean, median, standard deviation, and interquartile range). Use the 7‑point Likert scale uniformly; no data standardization is required.

steps.title: Provide feedback and run second Delphi round
steps.instruction: Create a second‑round questionnaire in Word. For each panelist, provide personalized feedback consisting of (a) a histogram showing the aggregated group response, (b) the panelist’s own estimate, and (c) a summary of the rationale extracted from panelists’ comments. Include feedback on all projections, even those that already reached consensus. Distribute the questionnaire by email and collect the completed forms.

steps.title: Determine consensus
steps.instruction: Apply an interquartile range (IQR) threshold of ≤ 1 to identify projections that achieved consensus. Use IQR together with mean, median, standard deviation, and the percentage change in standard deviation between rounds to assess convergence. Generate visual summaries: boxplots (to spot outliers), scatter plots (to explore possible clusters), and histograms of mean, minimum, and maximum values.

steps.title: Cluster projections into scenarios
steps.instruction: Using R, conduct cluster analysis on the seven projections that met the IQR ≤ 1 criterion. Base clustering on the means of probability, impact, and desirability for each projection. Compare four algorithms—fuzzy c‑means (FCM), k‑means, partitioning around medoids (PAM), and hierarchical clustering (HC). Determine the optimal number of clusters with the NbClust package employing Charrad et al.’s majority‑rule method. Because the dataset is small, select hierarchical clustering (Ward method with Euclidean distance) as the most appropriate. Produce a dendrogram to visualise the cluster structure.

steps.title: Define three future scenarios
steps.instruction:
Interpret the three hierarchical clusters as distinct scenarios:
1. **Personalized D2D travel** – projections 1, 4, 6, 10; Probability 6.045, Impact 0.815, Desirability 0.462.
2. **Integrated D2D travel** – projections 5, 14; Probability 6.296, Impact 0.085, Desirability 0.973.
3. **Game changer** – projection 16; Probability 4.535, Impact 0.114, Desirability 0.18.
Describe each scenario using panelists’ qualitative comments together with insights from the literature review and expert interviews.

steps.title: Create managerial insights and disseminate
steps.instruction: Derive practical implications for the main stakeholder groups (airports, airlines, public‑transport providers) based on the three scenarios. Use incentives such as distributing the study’s final results (a short, comprehensive summary with references) to thank panelists. Prepare visualisations of the scenarios (e.g., the figure shown in the original article) to aid communication. Send the summary and visual materials to all panelists.

description: The Delphi technique, first proposed in the 1950s, was developed by the RAND company [12]. It is an anonymous survey technique conducted in several rounds for structuring group communication. Panel participants are asked to assess projections (also called Delphi statements, questions or hypotheses) repeatedly [29], [30]. The Delphi method has four key characteristics: anonymity, iteration, controlled feedback, and statistical “group response” [43]. Beyond the classical Delphi approach [12], different types exist, such as the nominal group technique, decision Delphi, policy Delphi, and the argument Delphi [20], [38]. It is a suitable technique for answering prospective research questions of what the future might look like (as done in this study) and for instance to assess the expected probability, desirability and expected impact of projections or scenarios. The technique can also focus on current challenges, such as be used to rank and prioritize topics, support policy making, generating ideas, establishing facts, and for other research purposes. Items can also include an assessment on the feasibility, urgency for action, or innovativeness. It is applied mainly in the fields of healthcare, education and business research, with a significant increase in Delphi studies since 2005 [15]. An overview of the most cited papers across the disciplines is provided in the supplementary material (Table 2). Depending on the study type, the Delphi method follows a qualitative, quantitative or mixed-methods approach [38]. The technique can be combined with other methods, for instance to complement the development of projections or to support the analysis of results. There are also differences in the optimal number of panelists, number of rounds, consensus measurement, types of feedback loop and other parameters, giving rise to numerous modified Delphi versions [38], [54] that we believe may be overwhelming for researchers.
